title: Taser use queried in man's death
article: After Amnesty International slammed B.C. police forces when two people died in custody after being shot with Tasers, a friend of another man who died in a similar manner is also questioning the use of the disabling device.
Roman Andreichikov died May 1. His friend Rahim Hadini says Andreichikov, who was suicidal and high on cocaine, died shortly after he was shot in the chest with a Taser gun.
Tasers, which emit an electrical shock, are used to disable suspects but are not supposed to be lethal.
Hadini, who called 911 for an ambulance after his friend twice threatened to jump off a balcony, said Vancouver police were first at the scene.
"When they came in, they already had the Taser out," Hadini said.
Hadini claimed Andreichikov had obeyed police orders to lie face down on the floor but was shot in the chest after he rolled over. Within minutes, the fitness instructor was dead, he said.
This week, Amnesty International called for a suspension of the use of Taser guns by police, citing two other fatalities in B.C. as reason to question the safety of the disabling device.
Vancouver police confirm that a Taser was used to subdue Andreichikov, who was suicidal after a long drug binge and that an investigation into his death is ongoing.
While Taser manufacturers insist the stun guns are safe, an Amnesty spokeswoman says the growing number of in-custody fatalities where Tasers were used are cause for concern.
"That particular type of police equipment has not been researched enough," said campaigner Hilary Homes.
In the United States, where the use of Tasers is widespread, Amnesty has documented many cases of misuse and deaths related to heart attacks in cases where Tasers were used, she said.

Amnesty also questioned two other Canadian deaths and highlighted them this week in its 2004 human rights report -- Terry Hanna, in Burnaby and Clayton Alvin Willey, in Prince George. Both men were hit with Tasers during their arrests. Coroners' inquests in the two cases have yet to be held.
Steve Tuttle, spokesman for Taser International, the company which supplies virtually all North American police departments with Taser guns, said Tasers have been widely used since since 1999.
"We have never been cited as a cause of death," Tuttle said.

Tuttle said many arrests involving Tasers are complicated by drug use. In cases where suspects are in a state of excited delirium, their hearts race and they are prone to violent struggles and over exertion. But it is the heart attack, not the Taser jolt that kills, he said.
